name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)

lead: FWHR is the width of the face across the cheekbones divided by the height from upper lip to brow. Looksmaxxing users measure it from photos and treat a wider value as a stronger, more masculine and imposing face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it.

Researchers have studied it since the late 2000s as a cue of dominance and aggression. A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio larger in men than women with a small effect (d = 0.11), and another found a small positive link with men's aggression; some studies have not replicated this, and scientific work often links higher values with perceived threat. A study of adolescents found no association with testosterone levels.

paras: People measure FWHR from a straight-on photo and compare it with community targets. They then adjust what they can, such as facial hair, hairstyle and leanness, which change how wide or narrow the face reads.

Measuring is harmless, though camera distance and lens change the measured value. Cosmetic or hormonal approaches to widen the face, including among minors, are medical interventions, and no study shows that treatments change FWHR.

angle.text: Forum users calculate fWHR from photos and treat a higher ratio as a sign of a stronger, more masculine face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it. Research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression.

lead: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR or fWHR) is the distance between the cheekbones (bizygomatic width) divided by the height of the upper face, typically measured between the upper lip and the brow.[1][2] It is a size-independent measure and has been studied as a possible sexually dimorphic cue linked to dominance, threat and aggression.[1][2]

A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio was larger in men than in women, with a small effect size (d = 0.11).[1] A separate 2015 meta-analysis reported a small but significant positive relationship between men's FWHR and aggression.[2] Other work has found the link depends on factors such as income, and some studies have not replicated it.[3]

In looksmaxxing, FWHR became a standard metric. Grokipedia says community sources treat values around 1.8 or above as ideal for masculinity, while noting these are informal standards, and that scientific studies connect higher FWHR with perceived dominance and threat and often lower attractiveness ratings.[4]

paras: A 2008 study of hockey players and laboratory tasks reported that FWHR was associated with aggressive behavior.[5] A 2009 paper found observers could estimate aggression from neutral faces and that the estimates tracked FWHR.[6] A neuroimaging study reported amygdala reactivity to angry faces related to aggression only among men with larger FWHR.[7] A 2012 paper linked facial structure with unethical behavior.[8]

Later work questioned these findings. A 2018 study found FWHR was linked to dominance depending on income and testosterone and noted failures to replicate the aggression link.[3] A 2016 study found FWHR was not associated with adolescent testosterone levels, prompting commentaries and a response.[9] A 2023 study suggested observer bias plays a role: participants asked to draw or edit aggressive-dominant fictitious males produced faces with wider proportions.[10]

No studies found of FWHR in a clinical treatment setting, such as a trial testing an intervention that changes it. The research above is observational and experimental psychology: meta-analyses report a small sex difference and a small association with aggression in men, with mixed replication.[1][2][3]

Researchers have shown that photograph focal length changes depicted facial shape and perception.[11] A looksmax.org user reported that his FWHR measured about 1.75 to 1.8 from close range but about 2.0 from a long distance, and another replied that the measure is only useful at extremes.

Users post photos for FWHR calculation, debate what counts as high or low and discuss whether bone width can change in puberty. Grokipedia describes the numeric targets as informal community standards rather than validated criteria.[4]
